sentences.text: The name Yungavolucris brevipedalis translates to "Short-footed Yungas bird".
Known fossil specimens are small, measuring just over 4 cm in length.
The tarsometatarsals are unusually stout, flat, and very wide at the lower end.
Metatarsal IV is very thin and diminished but is about the same length as metatarsal III.
Metatarsal II possesses a very broad and pulley-shaped trochlea, which is the toe joint.
A small bony bump, known as a dorsomedial projection, is located just above the inside edge of the trochlea on metatarsal II.
No metatarsal I or hallux has been preserved in any Yungavolucris specimens.
Fossil bones of Yungavolucris were discovered in the Lecho Formation at estancia El Brete, Argentina.
Researchers suggest that if the legs were only shortened but not widened, Yungavolucris might have been a large chicken-sized bird that was heavily built, sluggish, and possibly flightless.
Yungavolucris belongs to the subclass Enantiornithes.
Some studies have recovered Yungavolucris as a close relative of Grabauornis.
The genus Yungavolucris was described by Chiappe in 1993.
Yungavolucris is an extinct genus of avialans belonging to the clade Enantiornithes that inhabited Argentina during the Upper Cretaceous.
Yungavolucris brevipedalis lived during the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian), approximately 70.6 to 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether Yungavolucris is the same species as other El Brete enantiornitheans known only from forelimb bones, since only the tarsometatarsus is known for Yungavolucris.
